I am a PhD candidate in Education Policy at the University of Virginia and an Institute of Education Sciences (IES) pre-doctoral fellow. My research answers two questions that arise whenever a new technology is deployed at scale: **does it work**, and **can we trust how we measure it?** I approach the first with causal inference and program evaluation — quasi-experimental designs, within-study comparisons, and policy-relevant estimands — and the second with measurement science: psychometric modeling, generalizability theory, and instrument validation.

My dissertation applies both toolkits to emerging technology in schools. One chapter evaluates a hybrid tutoring program that pairs adaptive learning software with live virtual tutoring, developing an "estimand ladder" that carries a regression discontinuity estimate from the eligibility cutoff to the full assigned population. Another develops a reliability framework for scores produced by large language model classifiers, showing how to select LLM scoring systems that yield dependable measurements of human behavior — with classroom observation as the application.

While my applied work centers on education, the underlying problems — extrapolating causal effects beyond where they are best identified, and quantifying the reliability of AI-generated measurements — are general. I build statistical software in Stata/Mata and work in R and Python.
